instances.brief: {{node_name}} and all its dependencies share a single availability zone. Everything you run sits in us-east-1a. An AZ outage would take the whole system down.
instances.teaches: Redundancy protects against a failure domain, not against a count. Two instances in one availability zone share the zone's fate.

wrong_outcomes.shows: us-east-1a goes dark in the drill. Both app instances are unreachable. Uptime drops 4.1%.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: The new instance shares the failing zone with the old one, so it fails at the same moment.

instances.reveal: An availability zone is a failure domain — power, network and cooling are shared inside it. Adding capacity within the same zone raises throughput but not survivability. The new instance belongs in us-east-1b, connected to the same load balancer so traffic can shift to it when 1a fails. It connects to both the load balancer, so traffic can reach it, and pg-primary, because an app instance with no datastore serves nothing.

instances.brief: {{node_name}} is routing cross-region writes through us-east-1. Your EU stack (lb-eu-01, app-eu-01) routes all writes to pg-primary in us-east-1. Last month a 23-minute us-east-1 outage caused 100% EU write failures despite EU compute staying healthy.
instances.teaches: A regional deployment is only as resilient as its most remote dependency. Cross-region writes re-centralise your failure domain across the wire regardless of where your compute lives.

wrong_outcomes.shows: eu-west-1a goes dark. app-eu-01 and the new database are in the same availability zone, so both vanish together. EU traffic fails over to us-east-1 across the Atlantic; p95 for EU users rises from 40 ms to 310 ms.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Placing the new database in app-eu-01's own zone gives you geographic separation from us-east-1 but no separation from the app tier it serves. A single AZ failure takes both.

instances.reveal: The trap here is geographic confusion: the new component is in Europe, so the EU stack looks independent. But if app-eu-01 still writes to pg-primary in us-east-1, the transatlantic link remains a single point of failure. The correct placement puts pg-replica in eu-west-1b — inside the EU region, but a different availability zone from app-eu-01, so an AZ failure does not take the app tier and its database together — and connects it to both app-eu-01 (the local write client) and pg-primary (the replication source). During a us-east-1 outage the EU database is promoted to accept writes locally; on recovery the two are reconciled and replication is re-established. Promotion is the step that makes the local write path real — a replica left in read-only mode fails EU writes exactly as the transatlantic dependency did. The failure domain is broken by moving the write dependency local — not just by placing a component in a new geography.

instances.brief: {{node_name}}'s primary Redis instance lives in us-east-1a with no replica. A zone failure would expose the application to cache miss storms — every request would fall through to the origin database simultaneously. Add a Redis standby in a second availability zone.
instances.teaches: Standbys protect against zone failures, not instance failures. The standby must be in a different AZ and must replicate directly from the primary — not from the application tier, which has no replication role.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Replication does not establish. Either the standby is in the same zone as the primary (both fail together on a zone outage) or it is connected to the application server rather than the primary (no replication path exists).
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: The standby must be in a different AZ from the primary and connected directly to the primary for replication. Connecting to the app tier or load balancer provides no data replication.

instances.reveal: A Redis standby requires: (1) a different availability zone from the primary, so a zone failure doesn't take both down; (2) a direct connection to the primary, so replication can establish. Connecting to app or lb instead of redis_primary leaves no replication path.

instances.brief: {{node_name}} runs in us-east-1. Your DR runbook requires a hot standby postgres in eu-west-1 that can serve reads within 60 seconds of a regional failure. The EU app stack (lb-eu, app-eu) is already deployed. Place the DR postgres replica and wire it into the EU stack.
instances.teaches: DR replicas must replicate directly from the primary — not from an existing replica, which adds replication lag and creates a chain dependency. The DR replica connects to the load balancer, which routes traffic during failover.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Either: replication lags because the DR replica is chained from pg-replica instead of pg-primary (replica-of-replica adds double the lag); or the EU load balancer cannot route to the DR postgres during failover because lb-eu was not wired to it.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: DR postgres must replicate from pg-primary directly (not pg-replica) and must be connected to lb-eu (not app-eu) so the EU load balancer can route traffic to it during a regional failover.

instances.reveal: DR postgres must replicate from pg-primary — not pg-replica, which adds lag and creates a chain dependency. It connects to lb-eu so the EU load balancer routes traffic to it during failover. Zone eu-west-1b provides geographic separation from eu-west-1a where lb-eu and app-eu already live.
